clinicalPearls: Congenital absence of the tricuspid valve with no direct connection between the right atrium and right ventricle
It is a cyanotic lesion and a form of functionally single ventricle
An obligatory atrial communication allows systemic venous blood to reach the left heart, and a ventricular septal defect or duct supplies pulmonary flow
Degree of cyanosis depends on the amount of pulmonary blood flow, which may be duct-dependent
The electrocardiogram often shows left-axis deviation with left ventricular dominance, unusual for a cyanotic newborn
Management follows the single-ventricle palliation pathway culminating in a Fontan circulation
reference.pathophysiology: In tricuspid atresia the absent tricuspid connection forces all systemic venous return to cross the atrial septum into the left atrium, where it mixes with pulmonary venous blood, producing cyanosis. The right ventricle is hypoplastic, and pulmonary blood flow depends on a ventricular septal defect, the arterial duct or associated lesions. Because a single functional (left) ventricle supports both circulations, the physiology and surgical approach follow the single-ventricle pathway, ultimately routing systemic venous blood directly to the lungs (Fontan).
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography defining the atretic valve and associated defects
Assessment of pulmonary blood flow and ductal dependence
redFlags: Severe cyanosis from inadequate pulmonary blood flow (duct closing)
Restrictive atrial septum impeding systemic venous egress
Excessive pulmonary flow causing heart failure
Failing Fontan circulation later in life
reference.prognosis: Staged single-ventricle palliation allows survival into adulthood for many, but the Fontan circulation carries long-term risks including arrhythmia, protein-losing enteropathy and circulatory failure.
pitfalls: Not maintaining ductal patency when pulmonary flow is duct-dependent
management: Stabilise the duct-dependent neonate with a prostaglandin E infusion to maintain ductal patency and pulmonary blood flow until intervention
Perform balloon atrial septostomy if the obligatory atrial communication is restrictive and limits systemic venous egress to the left heart
Pursue the staged single-ventricle palliation pathway, using an initial aortopulmonary shunt or pulmonary artery band as needed, then a bidirectional Glenn and finally Fontan completion
Give anticongestive therapy with diuretics for heart failure and institute antithrombotic therapy after Fontan completion to reduce thromboembolic risk

Undertake lifelong surveillance for Fontan complications including atrial arrhythmia, protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, thromboembolism, hepatic disease and ventricular dysfunction, with consideration of transplantation for the failing circulation
Support with nutrition, immunisations, endocarditis prophylaxis and individualised exercise advice

Manage through a paediatric and congenital cardiology and cardiac surgery team, with structured transition to adult congenital heart disease services and family counselling with foetal echocardiography in future pregnancies
